numberItems.stem: On a two-lane highway, a car coming toward you crosses the center line into your lane. Which way should you usually steer?
options: To the left, into the other driver's lane
To the right
Straight ahead while braking as hard as you can
numberItems.explanation: If an oncoming driver drifts into your lane, a move to your right is best; when that driver realizes the mistake, they will likely return to their own lane (p. 2-39).

numberItems.stem: You swerve onto a firm, clear shoulder at highway speed to avoid a crash. When should you start braking?
options: Right away, firmly, so you stop quickly
Not until you are down to about 5 mph
Once your speed drops to about 20 mph — then brake very gently
numberItems.explanation: If you leave the road, avoid braking until your speed has dropped to about 20 mph, then brake very gently to avoid skidding on the loose surface (p. 2-39).

numberItems.stem: You are forced back onto the road from the shoulder before you can stop. When do you countersteer?
options: As soon as both front tires are on the pavement
Only after all the wheels are back on the pavement
After edging back onto the road slowly and gradually
numberItems.explanation: Turn sharply enough to get right back on the road, and countersteer immediately when both front tires are on the paved surface (p. 2-39).

numberItems.stem: Which describes **controlled braking**?
options: Push the pedal as hard as you can and hold it until you stop
Brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels, keeping steering movements very small
Apply the brakes all the way, release when the wheels lock, and reapply when they roll
numberItems.explanation: Controlled braking means braking as hard as you can without locking the wheels, with very small steering movements. The third option is stab braking (p. 2-39).

numberItems.stem: Which describes **stab braking**?
options: Brake as hard as you can without locking the wheels
Release when the wheels lock, then reapply at once before they start rolling
Brake fully, release when the wheels lock, and brake fully again as soon as they start rolling
numberItems.explanation: Stab braking: apply the brakes all the way, release when the wheels lock, and reapply fully as soon as the wheels start rolling (p. 2-39).

numberItems.stem: In stab braking, after you release the brakes, it can take up to how long for the wheels to start rolling again?
options: 1 second
5 seconds
20 seconds
numberItems.explanation: It can take up to 1 second for the wheels to start rolling after you release; reapplying sooner means the vehicle won't straighten out (p. 2-39).

numberItems.stem: Your truck has working ABS on all axles. Should you use stab braking in an emergency?
options: Yes — stab braking works best with ABS
No — stab braking is only for vehicles without ABS
Yes, but only on the trailer brakes
numberItems.explanation: Stab braking can only be done in vehicles without ABS (p. 2-39). With working ABS on all axles you may fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop (p. 2-42).

numberItems.stem: Most hydraulic brake failures happen for which **2** reasons?
options: Wet brakes and worn brake linings
Loss of air pressure and an ABS malfunction
Loss of hydraulic pressure and brake fade on long hills
numberItems.explanation: Most hydraulic brake failures occur for one of 2 reasons: loss of hydraulic pressure or brake fade on long hills (p. 2-40).

numberItems.stem: Your hydraulic brake pedal suddenly feels spongy and goes to the floor. What has most likely happened?
options: The system has lost hydraulic pressure
The ABS has malfunctioned
A front tire has failed
numberItems.explanation: When the system will not build up pressure, the pedal feels spongy or goes to the floor — loss of hydraulic pressure (p. 2-40).

numberItems.stem: Where are runaway-truck escape ramps usually located?
options: Right at the crest of the grade
At the very bottom of the grade
A few miles from (below) the top of the downgrade
numberItems.explanation: Escape ramps are usually located a few miles from the top of the downgrade, and signs tell you they are coming (p. 2-40).

numberItems.stem: While driving, your steering suddenly feels "heavy." What is this most likely a sign of?
options: A rear dual tire has gone flat
A front tire has failed
The ABS has stopped working
numberItems.explanation: Heavy-feeling steering is probably a sign one of the front tires has failed; a flat rear tire more often shows up as vibration (p. 2-40).

numberItems.stem: DOT requires ABS on truck tractors **with air brakes** built on or after:
options: March 1, 1998
March 1, 1997
March 1, 1999
numberItems.explanation: Air-brake truck tractors: March 1, 1997. Other air-brake vehicles: March 1, 1998. Hydraulic trucks/buses 10,000 lb+ GVWR: March 1, 1999 (p. 2-41).

numberItems.stem: An air-brake **converter dolly** must have ABS if it was built on or after:
options: March 1, 1998
March 1, 1997
March 1, 1999
numberItems.explanation: Other air-brake vehicles — trucks, buses, trailers and converter dollies — built on or after March 1, 1998 must have ABS (p. 2-41).

numberItems.stem: A **hydraulic-brake** truck with a GVWR of 10,000 lb or more must have ABS if it was built on or after:
options: March 1, 1997
March 1, 1998
March 1, 1999
numberItems.explanation: Hydraulically braked trucks and buses with a GVWR of 10,000 pounds or more built on or after March 1, 1999 must have ABS (p. 2-41).

numberItems.stem: What color are ABS malfunction lamps on tractors, trucks, buses and trailers?
options: Red
Yellow
Blue
numberItems.explanation: ABS malfunction lamps are yellow (p. 2-41).

numberItems.stem: You are checking whether a trailer has ABS. Where should its malfunction lamp be?
options: On the right side, at the rear corner
On the tractor's instrument panel only
On the left side, at the front or rear corner
numberItems.explanation: Trailers have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner (p. 2-41).

numberItems.stem: On an **older** ABS system, the malfunction lamp may stay on after start-up until you are driving over:
options: 5 mph
20 mph
It should go out before you move — if not, ABS has failed
numberItems.explanation: On older systems the lamp could stay on until you are driving over 5 mph; on newer vehicles it goes out quickly after the bulb check (p. 2-41).

numberItems.stem: Your tractor has ABS but your trailer does not. You must make an emergency stop. How should you brake?
options: Fully apply the brakes — ABS on the tractor is enough
Use stab braking
Brake normally and watch the trailer — full application is only for working ABS on all axles
numberItems.explanation: Only a straight truck or combination with working ABS on all axles may fully apply the brakes in an emergency stop; otherwise brake normally and ease off if the trailer swings (p. 2-42).

numberItems.stem: Which list gives the handbook's causes of skids?
options: Over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast
Over-braking, worn brake linings, wet roads, and heavy loads
ABS failure, over-steering, under-inflated tires, and driving too fast
numberItems.explanation: Skids are caused in one of 4 ways: over-braking, over-steering, over-acceleration, and driving too fast (p. 2-42).

numberItems.stem: Which kind of skid is by far the most common?
options: Front-wheel skid
Drive-wheel (rear-wheel) skid
Trailer swing-out
numberItems.explanation: By far the most common skid is one in which the rear (drive) wheels lose traction through excessive braking or acceleration (p. 2-43).

numberItems.stem: According to the handbook, most serious skids result from:
options: Driving with ABS on only the tractor
Braking gently on dry pavement
Driving too fast for road conditions
numberItems.explanation: Most serious skids result from driving too fast for road conditions (p. 2-42).
